title: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
summary: Why hand-tuned prompts break, how APE, OPRO and DSPy search instructions and demos against a metric, why the dev-set winner is inflated, and what managed optimizers do.
outcomes: Explain why hand-tuned prompts are brittle across wording, format and models, citing measured effects
Describe how APE proposes and filters instructions and how OPRO's meta-prompt uses a scored trajectory
Explain DSPy signatures, modules and optimizers, including BootstrapFewShot traces and MIPROv2's search
Compute the standard error of a dev score and explain the winner's curse when selecting among many prompts
Set up train, validation and test splits and judge what a managed optimizer such as Bedrock actually measures

blocks.md:
From the prompting course you know the parts of a good prompt: rules, delimited inputs, a few examples, and room to reason. What that course could not tell you is **which** wording, which examples and which format will work best for *your* model on *your* task. Engineers usually find out by trial and error: edit, eyeball a handful of outputs, edit again.

This lesson shows why that loop is unreliable, and reframes prompt writing as a search problem that a program can run.

Kojima et al. found that adding a short **reasoning trigger** such as "Let's think step by step." before the answer makes a model reason before answering (zero-shot chain of thought). The APE paper (Zhou et al., ICLR 2023, Table 7) lists how much the exact trigger matters for InstructGPT (`text-davinci-002`) on MultiArith, a set of arithmetic word problems. The meaning of most triggers is nearly the same; the accuracy is not.

blocks.title: Zero-shot reasoning triggers on MultiArith (APE, Table 7)

scenes.caption: Accuracy of the same model on the same problems, changing only the trigger phrase. Without a trigger the model scores 17.7%.
Human-written triggers with similar meaning span 57.5% to 78.7%. Dropping the words "step by step" costs 21 points.
A trigger found automatically by APE, "Let's work this out in a step by step way to be sure we have the right answer.", beats the best human one: 82.0% versus 78.7%.

blocks.md:
Format matters as much as wording. Sclar et al. (ICLR 2024) varied only meaning-preserving formatting of few-shot prompts (separators, casing, spacing between fields) and saw accuracy differences of **up to 76 points** with LLaMA-2-13B. The sensitivity did not go away with larger models, more examples or instruction tuning, and which format was best only weakly correlated between models.

The best prompt is also **model-specific**. On GSM8K, APE's trigger beat "Let's think step by step." with InstructGPT (43.0% versus 40.7%), but when the OPRO paper re-tested both with PaLM 2-L, the APE trigger scored 58.8% against 71.8%.

Misconception: "a prompt that works is a good prompt". A hand-tuned prompt is fitted to one model, one task and the handful of examples you looked at. Change the model, the data or even the separator characters and the ranking of prompts can change.

The DSPy authors compare hand-tuned prompt strings to "hand-tuning the weights for a classifier". The fix is the same as in machine learning: define what good means as a number, collect examples, and let an algorithm search. **Automatic prompt optimization** has four ingredients:

1. A **search space**: the instruction text, the few-shot demonstrations, sometimes the format.
2. A **metric** that scores one output against one example (exact match, F1, a code check, or a validated LLM judge).
3. A **dev set** of examples to score candidates on.
4. A **proposer** that suggests new candidates (usually another LLM) and a **budget** of calls.

blocks.caption: APE's formulation (Zhou et al., Eq. 1): find the instruction rho that maximizes the average per-example score f of the target model's output on dataset D. No gradients are needed; the model is a black box.

blocks.title: Prompt optimization as a search loop

scenes.caption: The proposer LLM sees a few examples of the task and writes candidate prompts.
Each candidate is run by the target LLM on the dev set, and the metric scores every output. A candidate's score is its average.
Iterative methods feed the scores back so the next round builds on what worked. OPRO shows them to the proposer LLM; MIPRO feeds them to a Bayesian model that picks what to try next.
When the budget runs out, the highest-scoring candidate wins. Its dev score is biased upward because it was chosen for being high, so a separate test set gives the honest number.

blocks.prompt: You write 30 candidate prompts, score each on the same 20 dev examples, and pick the top scorer at 90%. Is 90% a fair estimate of what it will score in production?
blocks.reveal: No. With only 20 examples each score is noisy (one example is 5 points), and you picked the candidate whose noise happened to be most favourable. The winner's dev score is biased upward. This is the **winner's curse**, and lesson 4 measures it with a simulation. The cure is a held-out set that played no part in the choice.

blocks.md: Prompt optimization is search: candidates (instructions and demos), a metric, a dev set to score on, and a proposer. Everything else in this course is a choice of proposer, a way to spend the budget, or a way to keep the final number honest.

blocks.question: Your team tuned a prompt by hand to 91% on model X. Leadership switches to model Y. What does the evidence in this lesson suggest?
options: The prompt will keep roughly its 91% because its meaning has not changed
Re-run the search on model Y with the same metric and dev set, because the best prompt and format are model-specific
Add "You are an expert" to the prompt, since personas transfer across models
Only the few-shot examples need changing, never the instruction
blocks.explain: Sclar et al. found format performance only weakly correlates between models, and on GSM8K the APE trigger beat "Let's think step by step." with InstructGPT (43.0% versus 40.7%) but lost with PaLM 2-L (58.8% versus 71.8%). Keep the metric and data, and re-optimize for the new model.

blocks.question: Which ingredient, if missing, makes automatic prompt optimization impossible rather than just slower?
options: A large proposer model
Thousands of training examples
A metric that can score an output on an example
Access to the target model's gradients
blocks.explain: Search needs a way to compare candidates. Small dev sets work (OPRO used 3.5% of the GSM8K training set) and APE, OPRO and DSPy are all black-box, so no gradients are needed. Without a metric there is nothing to maximize.

lessons.title: APE and OPRO: language models that write prompts

blocks.md: **APE** (Automatic Prompt Engineer, Zhou et al., ICLR 2023) treats an instruction as a program to be synthesized from examples. Step one is **instruction induction**: show an LLM a few input-output pairs and ask it to infer the instruction. In the paper's main experiments it used five demonstrations per task and the forward template below.

blocks.code:
I gave a friend an instruction and five inputs. The friend read
the instruction and wrote an output for every one of the inputs.
Here are the input-output pairs:

Input: prove      Output: disprove
Input: on         Output: off
...

The instruction was <COMPLETE>
blocks.caption: APE's forward generation template (Figure 2 of the paper), filled here with antonym pairs from its Figure 1. The LLM completes the last line, and sampling it many times gives a pool of candidate instructions.

blocks.md:
Step two is **scoring**. Each candidate is prepended to held-in training inputs and run by the target model. APE uses either **execution accuracy** (1 if the output matches the label, else 0) or the **log probability** of the correct answer, $\log P(A \mid [\rho; Q])$, which gives a smoother signal when all candidates are weak.

Scoring every candidate on every example is expensive, so APE scores all candidates on a small subset, keeps the promising ones, scores those on a fresh non-overlapping subset, and repeats until a few remain for a full evaluation. Optionally, an LLM resamples variants of the best ones with "Generate a variation of the following instruction while keeping the semantic meaning."

blocks.title: APE on the antonym task (values from the paper's Figure 1)

scenes.caption: Four proposals from the demos, scored by negative log probability of the correct outputs (lower is better). Two proposals misread the task as string reversal.
Filter: keep the best scorers (lowest loss, here 0.26 and 0.28), discard the reversal ideas.
Optional resampling: an LLM writes semantic variants of a kept instruction, which are scored the same way.
Select the lowest loss: "write the opposite of the word given." at 0.16. The paper found such iteration gives only marginal gains, so plain APE skips it by default.

blocks.md: Results: with InstructGPT as the target, APE instructions matched or beat human-written ones on **24 of 24** Instruction Induction tasks and **17 of 21** curated BIG-Bench tasks. Pointed at zero-shot chain of thought, it found the trigger from lesson 1, which raised MultiArith from 78.7% to 82.0% and GSM8K from 40.7% to 43.0% over "Let's think step by step."

scenes.caption: The harness builds the meta-prompt: the best 20 instructions so far with their scores (ascending), 3 random training exemplars, and the meta-instructions.
The optimizer is sampled 8 times at temperature 1.0, giving 8 new candidate instructions. Several samples per step keep the search stable.
Each new instruction is inserted into the training questions and run by the scorer LLM at temperature 0 (greedy), so scores are repeatable.
Training accuracy is computed against the labels and the new (instruction, score) pairs join the trajectory. The next step's meta-prompt now includes them.
Repeat until no better instruction appears or the step budget runs out. Only then is the winner evaluated on the test set.

blocks.md: OPRO optimized on a small slice of data: **3.5%** of the GSM8K training set (about 260 problems) and 20% of each Big-Bench Hard task, then evaluated the found instruction on the full test set. The chart shows GSM8K test accuracy with pre-trained PaLM 2-L as the scorer (OPRO paper, Table 4).

blocks.title: GSM8K test accuracy, PaLM 2-L scorer (OPRO, Table 4)

scenes.caption: Baselines. The APE trigger that won on InstructGPT scores 58.8% here, below "Let's think step by step." at 71.8%.
Instructions found by OPRO: "Break this down." (PaLM 2-L as optimizer) at 79.9% and "Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step." (PaLM 2-L-IT as optimizer) at 80.2%.

blocks.md: Neither method needs gradients or weights: both only call model APIs. APE spends its budget on many independent proposals plus filtering; OPRO spends it on many sequential steps that each condition on the history. OPRO's authors note the trajectory makes the search sensitive to early low-quality candidates, which is why they sample 8 per step.

blocks.question: Which piece of information does OPRO's optimizer see that APE's proposal step does not?
options: The target model's log probabilities
A sorted list of earlier instructions with their measured scores
The test set labels
Gradients of the loss with respect to the prompt tokens
blocks.explain: OPRO's meta-prompt carries the optimization trajectory: past instructions and their training accuracies in ascending order. APE proposes from demonstrations, and its resampling only paraphrases a kept instruction. Neither method looks at test labels or gradients.

blocks.question: In APE's antonym example, two proposals read "reverse the input". Why does scoring on held-in examples, rather than just asking an LLM which instruction sounds best, catch this?
options: Because the metric runs the target model with each instruction and the reversal instructions produce wrong outputs
Because shorter instructions are always penalised
Because the proposer is forbidden from repeating words
It does not; APE relies on a human to remove them
blocks.explain: APE scores an instruction by what it makes the target model do: with "reverse the input" the model reverses letters, the correct antonyms get low probability, and the candidate is filtered out. Plausibility to a reader is not the objective; task performance is.

blocks.md: APE and OPRO optimize one instruction for one LLM call. Real systems chain calls: rewrite a query, retrieve, answer, check. **DSPy** (Khattab et al., Stanford, 2023) lets you write such a pipeline as a Python program and then **compile** it: an optimizer chooses instructions and demonstrations for every LLM call so that the whole program maximizes your metric. The project describes itself as a framework for programming, rather than prompting, language models. Three abstractions carry the idea.

A **signature** declares what one LLM call does: its input fields, output fields and an instruction. The short form is a string such as `"question -> answer"`. The class form adds types and a docstring; per the DSPy docs, the docstring becomes the task instructions, and without one DSPy writes "Given the fields X, produce the fields Y." Field types are validated with pydantic.

A **module** decides how to call the LM for a signature. `dspy.Predict` makes one call; `dspy.ChainOfThought` adds a reasoning field before the outputs; `dspy.ReAct` runs a tool-using loop. Modules compose like layers in PyTorch. Each `Predict` inside a program is a **predictor**, and its instruction and demos are the parameters an optimizer may change.

blocks.code:
from typing import Literal
import dspy

dspy.configure(lm=dspy.LM("provider/model-name"))

class Triage(dspy.Signature):
    """Classify a customer support ticket into one intent."""
    ticket: str = dspy.InputField()
    intent: Literal["billing", "bug", "account", "other"] = dspy.OutputField()

program = dspy.ChainOfThought(Triage)

def metric(example, pred, trace=None):
    return example.intent == pred.intent

optimizer = dspy.MIPROv2(metric=metric, auto="light")
compiled = optimizer.compile(program, trainset=train, valset=val)
compiled.save("triage.json")   # instructions and demos, per predictor
blocks.caption: A minimal DSPy program and compile step. train and val are lists of dspy.Example; the metric returns a bool or a number per example.

scenes.caption: Inputs: your program, a trainset (labels needed only for the final output) and a metric.
Search-based optimizers score candidate configurations on a valset. Pass one explicitly: for BootstrapRS the valset defaults to the trainset.
compile() returns a new program; the original is untouched. Its behaviour is fully described by each predictor's instruction and demos.
Compile once per program version, save, and serve the saved artifact. Inference is cheap; compilation is the expensive part.

blocks.md:
The simplest real optimizer is **BootstrapFewShot**. A teacher (by default a copy of your program; optionally a stronger one) runs on training examples. The metric checks each run, and the **traces** of passing runs (the inputs and outputs of every predictor along the way) become demonstrations. This is how DSPy gets demos for intermediate steps nobody labelled, such as a generated search query.

Per the docs, the defaults are `max_bootstrapped_demos=4` traced demos, with raw labelled examples filling the rest up to `max_labeled_demos=16` in total per predictor (so up to 12 raw), and the example being bootstrapped is removed from the teacher's demos first so it cannot copy its own answer.

blocks.title: BootstrapFewShot, simplified

scenes.caption: Start with no demos. Say max_bootstrapped is 2 for this toy.
Example 1: the teacher's run produces the right intent, so the whole trace (reasoning and answer) is kept.
Example 2: the run gives the wrong intent. The trace is thrown away, so bad reasoning never becomes a demo.
Example 3 passes. Two bootstrapped demos reached the cap, so the loop stops.
Remaining slots are filled with plain labelled examples (no reasoning), which the docs describe as ballast against bootstrap overfitting.

blocks.md:
Other optimizers in the current DSPy docs, grouped by what they tune:

- **Demos**: `LabeledFewShot` (random labelled examples, no LM calls, the honest baseline); `BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch` (alias `BootstrapRS`: runs the bootstrap with many seeds, 16 candidate programs by default, and keeps the best on the valset); `KNNFewShot` (picks demos per input at inference time).
- **Instructions**: `COPRO` (breadth x depth rounds of proposed instructions); `GEPA` (evolutionary search that reads textual feedback from the metric and reflects on failures).
- **Both**: `MIPROv2`. Also `SIMBA`, which targets the worst examples in each minibatch.
- **Weights**: `BootstrapFinetune` turns passing traces into fine-tuning data.

**MIPROv2** comes from MIPRO (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024). It works in three stages:

1. **Bootstrap** several candidate demo sets per predictor.
2. **Propose** candidate instructions per predictor with a prompt model that is shown a summary of the data, the program's code, sampled demos and a random prompting tip (grounded proposals).
3. **Search** combinations with Bayesian optimization (the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator sampling rule): each trial scores one combination on a random **minibatch** (35 examples by default) and updates the model of which choices are good; every few trials (5 by default) the best combination so far is scored on the full valset.

In the paper, MIPRO beat baseline optimizers on 5 of 7 diverse LM programs with Llama-3-8B, by up to 13% accuracy. The `auto` setting (`light`, `medium`, `heavy`) sets the budget.

blocks.title: DSPy paper, GSM8K with GPT-3.5 (Table 1): dev versus test

scenes.caption: Dev accuracy (300 dev problems) for three compiled chain-of-thought programs. Bootstrapped demos match expert human reasoning chains, and an ensemble of compiled programs reaches 88.3%.
On the 1.3k official test problems every number drops by 6 to 7.5 points: 72.4%, 72.9%, 81.6%. The dev set was used to make choices, so it flatters the result.

blocks.md: Every bootstrap and search optimizer trusts the metric. The DSPy docs warn that a non-deterministic metric (for example an LLM judge) makes the chosen demos "a function of metric noise as much as program quality". Make the metric deterministic where you can, validate any LLM judge against humans first, and keep a held-out set.

blocks.question: Your RAG program has a query-writer predictor and an answer predictor, but your data only labels final answers. How does BootstrapFewShot get demos for the query writer?
options: It cannot; you must hand-label good queries
It runs the whole program, and when the final answer passes the metric it keeps every predictor's input and output from that run as demos
It asks the proposer LLM to invent ideal queries without running the program
It fine-tunes the query writer on the answers
blocks.explain: Bootstrapping keeps full traces of runs that pass the metric, so intermediate steps get demos for free. That is the main reason DSPy needs labels only for the final output.

blocks.question: You want to tune both the instruction and the demos of each predictor, your metric returns only a number (no textual feedback), and you have a moderate budget. Which optimizer do the DSPy docs point to?
options: LabeledFewShot
KNNFewShot
BootstrapFinetune
MIPROv2
blocks.explain: MIPROv2 searches instructions and demos jointly with Bayesian optimization and treats the metric as a black-box scalar. GEPA is the other strong option but gets most of its power from textual feedback in the metric; LabeledFewShot and KNNFewShot only choose demos; BootstrapFinetune changes weights.

lessons.title: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse

blocks.md:
Time to run the selection step with numbers. The task is support ticket triage. We have **8 candidate instructions**: P1 is the hand-written prompt; P2 to P8 came from an APE-style proposer. We score each on a **dev set of 40 tickets** and keep the best.

To see what really happens we use a simulation (numbers computed by a script). We give each prompt a **true accuracy**, the rate it would achieve on unlimited tickets: P1 0.70, P2 0.74, P3 0.72, P4 0.77, P5 0.71, P6 0.75, P7 0.73, P8 0.69. In real life these are unknown; the dev score is a noisy estimate. P4 is truly best.

blocks.prompt: In one simulated run the hand-written P1 scores 0.70 on dev and the winner scores 0.80. If you ship the winner, how much better than P1 should you expect it to be on fresh tickets?
blocks.reveal: Much less than 10 points. On 500 fresh held-out tickets in this run, P1 scores 0.690 and the winner scores 0.720: a 3 point gain, not 10. And the winner is P5, whose true accuracy (0.71) is barely above P1's. Its dev score was lucky.

blocks.title: One simulated selection run (40 dev, 500 held-out)

scenes.caption: Dev accuracy of each candidate on the same 40 tickets. One ticket is worth 0.025, so these numbers move in coarse steps.
Selection picks the top dev score: P5 at 0.800 (32 of 40), a 10 point lead over the hand-written P1.
Held-out check on 500 fresh tickets, scored once: P5 gets 0.720 against P1's 0.690. The real gain is 3 points.
For teaching only, every prompt on the held-out set (never select with it). P4 scores 0.762, the best, yet it was ranked 7th of 8 on dev.
The true accuracies the simulation used. P5 is 0.71: the dev winner was chosen mostly for noise. Held-out scores land within 0.02 of truth because 500 items average out much better than 40.

blocks.md:
Why does this happen? A dev accuracy over $n$ examples has a **standard error** of about $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. With $p \approx 0.73$ and $n = 40$ that is 0.070, so two prompts that are truly 3 points apart are routinely reordered.

Selection makes it worse. Taking the maximum of $k$ noisy scores picks the candidate with the most favourable noise. If all $k$ candidates had the same true accuracy, the expected maximum of $k$ standard normal draws is about 0.56 for $k=2$, 1.42 for $k=8$ and 2.33 for $k=64$, so the winner's dev score overstates its truth by roughly that many standard errors.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: k candidates with equal true accuracy p, independent dev noise. c_k is the expected maximum of k standard normal draws (computed by simulation).

blocks.title: How much the winner's dev score overstates its truth

scenes.caption: k = 8 (c = 1.42). Dots are the average optimism over 4,000 simulated runs with our 8 prompts: 0.090 at n = 40, 0.031 at n = 200.
k = 64 (c = 2.33). Scoring more candidates on the same small dev set inflates the winner further. Searches like OPRO and MIPRO try many candidates.
k = 2 (c = 0.56). Fewer candidates or a larger dev set both shrink the bias. The model overstates the dots at large n because our real candidates differ, so the best one wins more often on merit.

blocks.title: How often selection finds the truly best prompt (P4)

scenes.caption: Fraction of 4,000 simulated runs in which the dev winner is P4. With 40 dev examples it is under 0.3; even 400 examples find it only about 63% of the time, because P6 (0.75) is close behind.

blocks.md:
Real systems show the same gap. OPRO's authors report that training accuracies were often 5% to 20% higher than test accuracies, and suggest a larger training set and fewer optimization steps (early stopping). In the DSPy paper's GSM8K table (GPT-3.5), the three compiled chain-of-thought programs each lose 6 to 7.5 points from dev to test.

How to hold out data:

1. **Train split**: the pool demos are drawn and bootstrapped from.
2. **Validation split**: scores candidates and picks the winner. Pass it explicitly in DSPy.
3. **Test split**: touched once, at the end, to report the number. Never select with it, or it becomes a second validation set.
4. Score all candidates on the **same** items, so differences are not partly due to different items, and prefer more validation examples over more candidates when data is scarce. The DSPy docs add that demo tuning tends to overfit small sets more than instruction tuning.
The data that chose the prompt cannot also grade it. Report the selected prompt's score on a held-out set that played no part in any choice, and expect it to be lower than the dev score.

blocks.question: A colleague scores 64 OPRO candidates on 30 dev examples and reports the winner's 93% as the expected production accuracy. What is the best response?
options: Accept it: OPRO uses temperature 0 for scoring, so scores are exact
Accept it if the winner is shorter than the baseline
Ask for the winner's score on a held-out set, and use a larger validation set; with 64 candidates and 30 examples the winner's dev score is strongly inflated
Re-run OPRO with temperature 1.0 for the scorer
blocks.explain: Temperature 0 makes each score repeatable, not accurate: 30 examples still give a standard error near 0.05 per prompt, and the best of 64 is inflated by more than 2 standard errors in the equal-accuracy model. Only an untouched held-out set gives an unbiased estimate.

blocks.question: You run DSPy's BootstrapRS without passing a valset. It reports 0.92 on 50 training examples, and 0.81 on your test set. What most likely explains the gap?
options: The valset defaulted to the trainset, so demos were bootstrapped from and selected on the same examples
BootstrapRS always reports accuracy times 1.1
The test set must be mislabelled
Random search cannot overfit
blocks.explain: Per the DSPy docs the valset defaults to the trainset. The selected program contains demos drawn from those same examples and was chosen for scoring well on them, so its training score is optimistic. Pass a separate valset and keep a test set apart.

lessons.title: Managed prompt optimizers and a practical workflow

blocks.md:
Cloud platforms now offer prompt optimization as a service. Amazon Bedrock documents two kinds, and the difference between them is exactly the difference between rewriting and optimizing.

**Simple prompt optimization** performs, in the docs' words, "a fast, heuristic rewrite of a single short prompt for one model". It works best for prompts of about 1k tokens or less, and it **does not use evaluation data**. Bedrock first analyzes the prompt's components and then rewrites it. In the console you press Optimize and compare original and rewrite side by side. Through the API you send an `OptimizePrompt` request with the prompt and a `targetModelId`, and receive a stream with an `analyzePromptEvent` and then an `optimizedPromptEvent`.

blocks.caption: Simple prompt optimization through the API, condensed from the AWS docs sample. TARGET_MODEL_ID is a Bedrock model ID.

blocks.md:
**Advanced Prompt Optimization (AdvPO)** is evaluation-driven. You supply prompt templates, example inputs for their variables (evaluation samples), ground-truth answers, and an evaluation method: an LLM-as-judge rubric, a Lambda function, or short natural-language steering criteria. The samples are run through your target model, graded, and the service rewrites the prompt and repeats; the docs say the loop ends "according to proprietary internal optimization parameters".

The docs also note that the optimizer reads your metric code, "source text and docstrings", to understand what good means, so a precise metric matters twice. You can compare the original and optimized prompts across several models at once, restrict rewriting to tagged sections of a template, and optionally shorten prompts. Results include before and after templates, per-sample scores, and latency and time-to-first-token figures. You pay for the inference and Lambda calls, with no separate service charge.

blocks.title: Bedrock: simple rewrite versus evaluation-driven loop

scenes.caption: Simple optimization: analyze, then rewrite, for one model. No data and no metric are involved, so nothing measures whether the rewrite is better.
Advanced optimization: your samples run on the target model and are graded by your evaluator. This is the same loop as lesson 1, run by the service.
The output reports scores per sample and latency per model. Those scores were used for the search, so still confirm on data the job never saw.

blocks.md: A rewrite produced without evaluation data is a hypothesis, not a result. Treat it like a candidate from a proposer: score it on your validation set against the current prompt before shipping.

A workflow that combines the course:

1. **Define the metric** first. If it is an LLM judge, validate it against human labels as in the LLM-as-judge course; every optimizer here will exploit its blind spots.
2. **Collect and split** examples into train, validation and test, sampled from real traffic and covering hard cases.
3. **Baseline**: score the current prompt, and a cheap optimizer such as `LabeledFewShot` or `BootstrapFewShot`.
4. **Search** with more budget (MIPROv2, GEPA, OPRO-style loops or a managed service) only if the baseline gap justifies it. The DSPy docs warn that a single MIPROv2 or GEPA run can cost hundreds of US dollars in LM calls.
5. **Report** the winner on the test set once, save the compiled prompt under version control, and **re-optimize when the model changes**.

blocks.question: Which statement about Amazon Bedrock's simple prompt optimization matches the AWS docs?
options: It searches over many candidates and returns the one with the best score on your data
It performs a fast heuristic rewrite of one prompt for one chosen model and does not use evaluation data
It fine-tunes the target model on your prompt
It guarantees the rewritten prompt scores higher on your task
blocks.explain: The docs describe simple optimization as a heuristic rewrite of a single short prompt for one model, with no evaluation data and no multi-model support. Evaluation-driven optimization is the separate Advanced Prompt Optimization feature.

blocks.question: You move a production prompt that was optimized with DSPy for one model to a different model. Based on this course, what should you do?
options: Nothing: compiled prompts are model-independent
Only re-run the test set, never the optimizer
Re-compile against the new model with the same metric and splits, then compare both on the test set
Delete all demos, since demos never transfer
blocks.explain: Lesson 1 showed the best wording is model-specific: on GSM8K the APE trigger won with InstructGPT and lost by 13 points with PaLM 2-L. Keeping the metric and splits fixed makes the re-optimized prompt directly comparable with the old one.

blocks.question: Bedrock's Advanced Prompt Optimization reads your Lambda metric's source code and docstrings. What is the practical consequence?
options: Metric code is ignored if you also give ground truth
A vague or buggy metric steers the rewriting toward the wrong goal, so make the metric precise and test it before the job
You must write the metric in natural language only
The judge model will be fine-tuned on your docstrings
blocks.explain: The docs say both the dataset and the metric shape optimization quality, and that the evaluation steers the rewriting. Like every optimizer in this course, it maximizes what you measure, not what you meant.
